acid-reflux-gerd-guide.question: How do you treat acid reflux (GERD)?
acid-reflux-gerd-guide.answerHtml: GERD affects ~20% of U.S. adults weekly and is best managed per the 2022 ACG Clinical Guideline with a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) taken 30–60 minutes before a meal — omeprazole 20 mg or pantoprazole 40 mg daily — which suppresses acid production by 80–95% and heals erosive esophagitis. Famotidine 20–40 mg suits mild intermittent symptoms. Lifestyle changes — elevating the head of the bed, losing weight, and finishing meals at least 3 hours before bedtime — provide meaningful additive benefit, per the AAFP. Alarm symptoms (dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, hematemesis) require urgent endoscopy. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

acne-treatment-guide.question: What is the most effective treatment for acne?
acne-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Per the 2024 AAD acne guideline — the first major update since 2016 — combination therapy outperforms monotherapy. A standard regimen pairs topical tretinoin 0.025–0.05% nightly with benzoyl peroxide 2.5–5%, plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3–4 months in moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne. Spironolactone 50–100 mg daily is an antibiotic-sparing option for hormonal acne in women. Nodulocystic or scarring acne warrants dermatology referral for isotretinoin. Acne affects nearly 50 million Americans annually; undertreated disease causes permanent scarring and psychological harm. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

ai-chatbot-medical-information-safety.question: Is it safe to use AI chatbots like ChatGPT for medical information?
ai-chatbot-medical-information-safety.answerHtml: AI chatbots carry documented health information risks. A 2026 BMJ Open audit of five chatbots found 49.6% of 250 health responses were problematic; 19.6% were highly problematic or potentially harmful. Average reference completeness was only 40%, and a 2023 JMIR study found only 32% of AI-generated citations fully accurate, with nearly half partly fabricated. Chatbots pattern-match rather than reason clinically and rarely express uncertainty. Safe use rules: never rely on a chatbot to decide if a symptom needs emergency care; confirm diagnoses or drug decisions with a licensed clinician. A licensed clinician — reached via telehealth or an in-person visit — provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

ai-chatbots-vs-physicians-diagnostic-acc.question: How accurate are AI chatbots compared to physicians at diagnosing medical conditions?
ai-chatbots-vs-physicians-diagnostic-acc.answerHtml: A 2025 Nature Digital Medicine meta-analysis of 83 studies found AI chatbots achieve an overall diagnostic accuracy of 52.1% and trail expert specialist physicians by 15.8 percentage points. A 2026 Oxford study in Nature Medicine found patients using chatbots performed no better than those using a Google search; models produced a mix of accurate and misleading information users could not reliably separate. ECRI documented chatbots inventing body parts and suggesting dangerous device placements. A licensed clinician — reached via telehealth or an in-person visit — provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

ai-respiratory-symptom-triage.question: Can AI chatbots safely triage respiratory symptoms like shortness of breath or cough?
ai-respiratory-symptom-triage.answerHtml: Current evidence shows AI chatbots cannot safely triage breathing problems. A 2026 Nature Medicine study from Mount Sinai found 52% of genuine emergencies across 960 AI interactions were under-triaged — patients told to wait when urgent care was needed. Atypical pneumonia without fever was frequently missed; when a family member's reassuring framing was added, the AI was nearly 12 times more likely to downgrade urgency regardless of clinical facts. A 2026 JMIR systematic review confirmed promising research accuracy (AUC 0.82–0.94) but near-zero real-world primary care validation data. A licensed clinician — reached via telehealth or an in-person visit — provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

altitude-sickness-diamox-guide.question: How does Diamox (acetazolamide) prevent altitude sickness?
altitude-sickness-diamox-guide.answerHtml: Acetazolamide (Diamox) is the only FDA-approved pharmacological prophylaxis for acute mountain sickness (AMS). It works as a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — blocking the enzyme in the kidneys causes bicarbonate excretion and a mild metabolic acidosis, which stimulates the respiratory center to increase ventilation rate and depth, elevating arterial oxygen saturation and accelerating acclimatization. Per the CDC Yellow Book, the recommended prophylaxis dose is 125 mg twice daily starting 24 hours before ascent, continued for 2 days at maximum altitude. The Wilderness Medical Society guidelines confirm 125 mg BID equals the older 250 mg BID dose in efficacy with fewer side effects. Acetazolamide is contraindicated with sulfa allergy and in all trimesters of pregnancy.

anti-aging-treatment-guide.question: What anti-aging skin treatments actually work?
anti-aging-treatment-guide.answerHtml: The strongest evidence-based anti-aging interventions are daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen and prescription tretinoin. UV exposure drives 80–90% of visible skin aging; the American Academy of Dermatology recommends SPF 30+ applied daily year-round. A systematic review of seven RCTs found tretinoin 0.025–0.1% consistently improves wrinkling, hyperpigmentation, and lentigines with benefit at one month and maintained at 24 months; it requires a prescription. OTC retinol is ~10× weaker and slower. Vitamin C serum (L-ascorbic acid 10–20%) adds antioxidant protection. Procedures (chemical peels, lasers) address Grade III–IV photoaging and require in-person dermatology. Tretinoin and retinoids are contraindicated in pregnancy. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

anxiety-depression-medication-guide.question: What medications are used to treat anxiety and depression?
anxiety-depression-medication-guide.answerHtml: Anxiety disorders affect 19.1% and major depression 8.3% of U.S. adults, per the NIMH (2026). Per the APA clinical practice guideline and NICE NG222 (reviewed January 2026), SSRIs — sertraline 50–200 mg or escitalopram 10–20 mg daily — are first-line for both conditions, combined with psychotherapy for moderate-to-severe presentations. SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are alternatives when pain or anxiety predominate. Full response takes 4–6 weeks at adequate dose; side effects typically precede benefits. Never stop antidepressants abruptly — FDA and NICE guidance requires a gradual taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome (highest risk with paroxetine and venlafaxine). A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

asthma-guide.question: How is asthma treated according to the latest guidelines?
asthma-guide.answerHtml: Asthma affects 28 million Americans and causes over 3,000 preventable deaths annually, per the CDC. The GINA 2025 guideline mandates a landmark shift: no patient should use a short-acting beta-agonist (albuterol) alone — every patient needs ICS-containing therapy. For mild asthma, low-dose ICS-formoterol used as needed reduces severe exacerbations ~65% versus SABA alone. Moderate-to-severe disease is managed with daily ICS-LABA; SMART therapy (ICS-formoterol as both controller and reliever) cuts exacerbations ~30% versus separate inhalers. Alarm signs — peak flow below 50%, inability to speak in full sentences, no response to rescue inhaler — require emergency care. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

at-home-uti-test-guide.question: Are at-home UTI test strips accurate, and when should I trust the result?
at-home-uti-test-guide.answerHtml: At-home UTI dipsticks measure two chemical signals, nitrite and leukocyte esterase. Pooled from Devillé 2004 and St John 2006, combined sensitivity in symptomatic women is roughly 68 to 88% and combined specificity is roughly 82 to 90%. That makes a positive strip useful for raising pre-test probability in young premenopausal women with classic symptoms, but a negative strip does not rule out UTI (nitrite-negative organisms like Enterococcus and Staphylococcus saprophyticus are common). Performance falls further in older adults; a fresh 2026 meta-analysis found dipstick specificity of only 39% for predicting UTI in symptomatic older adults. The 2025 AUA/CUA/SUFU recurrent-UTI guideline does not advocate home dipstick testing for recurrent UTI diagnosis. Skip the strip entirely if you have red flags (fever, flank pain, visible blood, pregnancy, symptoms >7 days, or new symptoms in a man). For everyone else, contact a licensed clinician for evaluation. A telehealth visit is often the fastest evidence-based path to a treatment decision.

azo-home-uti-test-strips-review.question: How accurate are AZO Home UTI Test Strips, and what do the results mean?
azo-home-uti-test-strips-review.answerHtml: AZO Home UTI Test Strips measure leukocyte esterase and nitrite, not bacteria directly. In the Devillé meta-analysis, leukocyte esterase alone had sensitivity of about 48 to 86% and nitrite alone 45 to 60%; a nitrite-positive result is relatively specific, while a negative strip does not rule out UTI. A positive leukocyte result with negative nitrite can reflect an early UTI, a nitrite-negative organism such as Enterococcus or Staphylococcus saprophyticus, contamination, or another cause of urinary inflammation. Read the strip within the package window, generally 60 to 120 seconds, not after five minutes. A positive strip with urinary symptoms should prompt clinical assessment; fever, flank pain, vomiting, pregnancy, recurrent symptoms, or urinary symptoms in a man call for medical care rather than reliance on a home test.

bacterial-vaginosis-bv-guide.question: How is bacterial vaginosis (BV) treated?
bacterial-vaginosis-bv-guide.answerHtml: Bacterial vaginosis affects ~21 million U.S. women annually; untreated BV increases risk of HIV/STI acquisition, pelvic inflammatory disease, and preterm birth, per the CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines. First-line options (all ~90% cure rates): metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily × 7 days, or metronidazole 0.75% vaginal gel × 5 days, or clindamycin 2% cream × 7 days. Avoid alcohol during and 24 hours after oral metronidazole. Up to 66% of women recur within 12 months; suppressive vaginal metronidazole gel is recommended for ≥3 episodes per year. A 2025 NEJM RCT showed treating male partners cut 12-week recurrence from 63% to 35%. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

birth-control-refills-guide.question: Do you need a doctor's visit to refill hormonal birth control?
birth-control-refills-guide.answerHtml: No routine exam is required to refill hormonal contraception. The 2024 CDC U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria and ACOG state only a blood pressure check is needed for combined methods; progestin-only methods require no testing at all. The 2024 CDC U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations explicitly note that restricting supply to 1–3 month quantities is a barrier to effective contraception — annual supply improves continuation and reduces unintended pregnancy. Seek emergency care for sudden leg swelling, chest pain, severe headache, or visual changes — possible signs of VTE or stroke. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

cat-bite-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a cat bite?
cat-bite-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Cat bites carry a 30–50% infection rate — far higher than dog bites — because feline teeth create deep puncture wounds that seal bacteria into tissue, per the IDSA SSTI Guidelines. Pasteurella multocida, present in ~90% of cat oral flora, can produce cellulitis within 3–6 hours. Prophylactic antibiotics are standard for all cat bites: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 5–7 days (use doxycycline 100 mg twice daily if penicillin-allergic). Hand bites require same-day evaluation — cat teeth can penetrate flexor tendon sheaths, causing pyogenic tenosynovitis, a surgical emergency. Per CDC animal bite guidance, go to the ER for Kanavel signs, fever, or rapid spread. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

cellulitis-guide.question: How is cellulitis treated?
cellulitis-guide.answerHtml: Cellulitis — bacterial infection of the deep dermis — accounts for over 14 million U.S. outpatient visits annually. Per the IDSA 2014 SSTI Guidelines, non-purulent mild cellulitis is treated with cephalexin 500 mg four times daily or dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5–7 days; add trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline if MRSA is suspected. Mark the redness border at treatment initiation — advancement past the line at 48 hours despite antibiotics signals failure. Fever, hypotension, or rapid spread requires IV antibiotics and hospitalization. Notably, up to 30% of cellulitis diagnoses are actually venous stasis dermatitis or DVT — correct diagnosis matters. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

chlamydia-treatment-guide.question: What is the CDC-recommended treatment for chlamydia in 2025?
chlamydia-treatment-guide.answerHtml: The CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines moved doxycycline to first-line status, replacing azithromycin: doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days achieves 100% cure for rectal chlamydia versus 74% with azithromycin, per a landmark Clinical Infectious Diseases RCT. Rectal co-infection occurs in 33–83% of women with urogenital chlamydia and serves as a re-seeding reservoir — making doxycycline the superior choice for all anatomic sites. In pregnancy, azithromycin 1 g single-dose remains preferred (doxycycline is contraindicated). The USPSTF recommends annual screening for all sexually active women ≤24 and at-risk women ≥25. Abstain for 7 days post-treatment until all partners are treated. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

cholesterol-hyperlipidemia-guide.question: What are the 2026 ACC/AHA guidelines for treating high cholesterol?
cholesterol-hyperlipidemia-guide.answerHtml: The 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia Guideline reintroduces specific LDL-C targets: <100 mg/dL for intermediate risk, <70 mg/dL for high risk, and <55 mg/dL for very-high-risk secondary prevention. It replaces the Pooled Cohort Equations with the PREVENT-ASCVD calculator and adds a Class I recommendation to measure lipoprotein(a) at least once per lifetime. High-intensity statins — rosuvastatin 20–40 mg or atorvastatin 40–80 mg — are recommended for high-risk patients. A 2026 Lancet meta-analysis of 19 trials (>120,000 patients) confirmed only 4 of 66 listed statin side effects are genuinely drug-caused. About 86 million U.S. adults have total cholesterol above 200 mg/dL (2026). A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

chronic-conditions-visiting-parents-guid.question: How can I keep my visiting parents' chronic conditions stable during a US trip?
chronic-conditions-visiting-parents-guid.answerHtml: For older international visitors with chronic conditions like hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, atrial fibrillation, COPD, or asthma, the four things that keep a US trip uneventful are a pre-travel visit with the home clinician 4 to 6 weeks before departure, the correct time-zone dosing plan for daily medications, all prescriptions packed in original containers in carry-on luggage with a written medication list, and a low threshold to use US telehealth for a same-day check-in when something feels off. The CDC Yellow Book specifically recommends pre-travel medical assessment for anyone with a chronic condition and states that chronic conditions should be under optimal control before travel. For short-haul trips of fewer than 5 time zones or fewer than 3 days, most oral daily medications and basal insulin do not need dose changes. For medium- and long-haul travel across 5 or more time zones for 3 or more days, basal insulin doses are adjusted by approximately 4 percent per time zone crossed (increase westbound, decrease eastbound, per Forst et al. 2021). Levothyroxine can be safely shifted to bedtime dosing at destination time, which simplifies time-zone transitions and is supported by Bolk et al. 2010 Arch Intern Med. For persistent post-flight jet lag in a healthy older visitor, a short course of melatonin 3 to 5 mg at destination bedtime for the first several nights has moderate evidence for eastward travel across 5 or more time zones per BMJ DTB 2020 and the CATMAT Statement on Older Travellers.

cold-and-flu-guide.question: How do you treat a cold or the flu, and how can you tell them apart?
cold-and-flu-guide.answerHtml: Influenza caused ~51 million U.S. illnesses and 45,000 deaths in 2024–2025, per the CDC. Flu onset is abrupt — high fever and myalgia within hours; colds develop gradually over 1–2 days. Per the IDSA Influenza Treatment Guidelines, high-risk patients (age ≥65, pregnancy, chronic cardiopulmonary or immunosuppressive conditions) should receive oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily × 5 days within 48 hours of onset; antiviral treatment remains recommended beyond 48 hours for hospitalized or severely ill patients. For colds, zinc acetate/gluconate lozenges (>75 mg elemental zinc/day) started within 24 hours shorten duration ~33%. Seek ER care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, or altered mental status. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

cold-sores-hsv1-guide.question: How do you treat a cold sore (HSV-1)?
cold-sores-hsv1-guide.answerHtml: Cold sores are caused by HSV-1, which infects an estimated 3.8 billion people under age 50 worldwide (WHO). Treatment is most effective when started during the prodromal tingling stage — ideally within 24 hours. AAFP-reviewed oral antivirals include valacyclovir 2 g twice daily for 1 day (episodic) or valacyclovir 500 mg daily for suppression, reducing recurrence by 70–80% (2026). Seek emergency care if a cold sore spreads near the eyes or if you are immunocompromised. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

contact-dermatitis-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat contact dermatitis?
contact-dermatitis-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Contact dermatitis has two types: irritant (direct chemical damage) and allergic (type IV delayed hypersensitivity). Per the AAD (2026), first-line treatment is removing the offending substance and applying a topical corticosteroid — high-potency for palms/soles, low-potency for the face. AAFP guidelines support short oral steroid courses for severe or widespread reactions. Patch testing confirms allergic contact dermatitis. Nickel, fragrance, and rubber accelerators are the most common allergens. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

covid-19-paxlovid-treatment-guide.question: Who should take Paxlovid for COVID-19 and how does it work?
covid-19-paxlovid-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) is the CDC's first-line oral antiviral for COVID-19 (2026), reducing hospitalization and death by 87–89% in clinical trials. It must be started within 5 days of symptom onset and is indicated for adults with at least one risk factor for severe disease — age ≥65, obesity, diabetes, or immunosuppression. The ritonavir component is a potent CYP3A inhibitor, requiring dose adjustment for statins, anticoagulants, and cardiac medications. FDA prescribing guidance (2026) should be reviewed for all concurrent medications. Paxlovid rebound occurs in ~5–15% but is self-limiting. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

d-mannose-uti-guide.question: Does D-mannose actually work for preventing UTIs?
d-mannose-uti-guide.answerHtml: The largest and most rigorous D-mannose trial to date (Hayward 2024, N=598) found no meaningful reduction in UTI recurrence versus placebo, and the 2025 AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline amendment now states that D-mannose alone "may not be effective" for UTI prevention. Better-supported options depend on the situation. For peri- and postmenopausal women with recurrent UTIs, low-dose vaginal estrogen is the highest-yield choice with roughly 50 to 75% reduction and a Strong AUA recommendation; the FDA removed the boxed warning in November 2025. Standardized cranberry products (at least 36 mg PACs daily) reduce recurrence by about 30% per the 2023 Cochrane review. Methenamine hippurate 1 g twice daily was non-inferior to daily low-dose antibiotics in the ALTAR trial (BMJ 2022) and does not select for antibiotic resistance. Women with baseline fluid intake below 1.5 L/day benefit from an additional 1.5 L of water daily. Two new oral antibiotics, pivmecillinam (Pivya, 2024) and gepotidacin (Blujepa, 2025), expand treatment options when standard agents fail. Any of these can be discussed with a licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth.

dandruff-seborrheic-dermatitis-guide.question: How do you treat dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis?
dandruff-seborrheic-dermatitis-guide.answerHtml: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory condition driven by Malassezia yeast — not poor hygiene — affecting 3–5% of adults, with dandruff affecting up to 50% at some point. Per the AAD (2026), first-line OTC options include zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide 1%, or ketoconazole 1% shampoos. For moderate-to-severe cases, AAFP guidelines support prescription ketoconazole 2% or ciclopirox 1% shampoo. Facial involvement may require low-potency topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors. Seborrheic dermatitis requires ongoing maintenance therapy — most patients relapse without it. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

dental-pain-guide.question: What can a doctor prescribe for dental pain, and when are antibiotics needed?
dental-pain-guide.answerHtml: A telemedicine physician can manage dental pain as bridge care until dentist access is available but cannot perform dental procedures. The 2024 ADA guideline recommends ibuprofen 400–600 mg combined with acetaminophen 500–1000 mg as first-line — outperforming opioids with fewer side effects. ADA antibiotic guidelines (2026) reserve antibiotics for dental infections with systemic signs: fever, facial swelling, or difficulty swallowing. Amoxicillin 500 mg TID for 5–7 days is first-line; clindamycin is no longer recommended due to C. difficile risk. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

dog-bite-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a dog bite wound and prevent infection?
dog-bite-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Dog bites carry a 5–15% infection risk from polymicrobial flora including Pasteurella canis. Per the CDC, immediate care requires washing with soap and water for at least 5 minutes. AAFP guidelines (2026) recommend amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 3–5 days for high-risk wounds: hand bites, deep punctures, wounds requiring primary closure, or immunocompromised patients. Rabies risk is low for vaccinated domestic dogs — apply the 10-day observation rule. Tetanus booster (Tdap) is indicated if last dose was more than 5 years ago. Go to the ER for deep facial lacerations or suspected tendon involvement. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

ear-infection-guide.question: How do you treat an ear infection in adults and children?
ear-infection-guide.answerHtml: Ear infections divide into middle ear (otitis media) and outer ear (otitis externa/swimmer's ear) — different pathogens, different treatments. AAP guidelines (2026) support watchful waiting 48–72 hours for mild unilateral otitis media in children over 6 months; roughly two-thirds resolve without antibiotics. When treatment is indicated, amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day is first-line; amoxicillin-clavulanate for treatment failures. AAFP guidelines recommend topical antibiotic-steroid drops (ofloxacin or ciprofloxacin/dexamethasone) as first-line for otitis externa. Seek emergency care for post-auricular swelling, facial weakness, or sudden hearing loss. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

eczema-atopic-dermatitis-guide.question: How is eczema (atopic dermatitis) treated in 2026?
eczema-atopic-dermatitis-guide.answerHtml: Eczema (atopic dermatitis) is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by skin barrier dysfunction, affecting over 31 million Americans. The 2025 AAD focused update added four new strongly recommended therapies: tapinarof cream, roflumilast cream, lebrikizumab, and nemolizumab. Treatment follows a step-up ladder: moisturization and trigger avoidance → topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors → phototherapy → biologics (dupilumab) or JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, abrocitinib) for moderate-to-severe disease. NEJM trial data show dupilumab achieves clear/nearly-clear skin in ~38% at 16 weeks. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

epinephrine-auto-injector-guide.question: How do you use an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) and when is it needed?
epinephrine-auto-injector-guide.answerHtml: Epinephrine is the only first-line treatment for anaphylaxis — antihistamines do not stop a systemic allergic reaction. Per the AAAAI/ACAAI 2023 Practice Parameter, anaphylaxis involves two or more organ systems after allergen exposure. Adult dose: 0.3 mg IM into the outer mid-thigh; children 15–30 kg receive 0.15 mg. Carry two devices — if symptoms persist after 5–15 minutes, use the second and call 911. Only 11% of patients self-administer epinephrine during a reaction, contributing to ~225 anaphylaxis deaths annually in the U.S. Always go to the ER after use — biphasic reactions can occur up to 72 hours later (ACAAI). A licensed clinician — reached via telehealth or an in-person visit — provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

erectile-dysfunction-guide.question: What is the best treatment for erectile dysfunction in 2026?
erectile-dysfunction-guide.answerHtml: Erectile dysfunction affects roughly 30 million U.S. men and is primarily a vascular condition. A 2023 JACC Advances umbrella review found ED independently predicts cardiovascular disease (RR 1.45), coronary heart disease (RR 1.50), and stroke (RR 1.36), which is why the 2024 Princeton IV Consensus treats ED as a cardiovascular risk-enhancing factor. First-line treatment per the AUA guideline (2018, reaffirmed 2025) and the EAU 2026 guideline is a PDE5 inhibitor: sildenafil 50 mg PRN, tadalafil 10 mg PRN or 5 mg daily, vardenafil 10 mg PRN, or avanafil 100 mg PRN. Generic sildenafil now costs about $0.50 to $1.50 per dose. A 2023 Journal of Sexual Medicine meta-analysis shows aerobic exercise improves IIEF-EF scores by roughly 2.8 points. Testosterone therapy in hypogonadal men is cardiovascular-neutral per the 2023 NEJM TRAVERSE trial. Over-the-counter "male enhancement" supplements are unregulated and frequently contain hidden PDE5 inhibitors per FDA safety notifications. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review symptoms, screen cardiovascular risk, and prescribe appropriate therapy.

fda-compounded-glp1-503b-proposal.question: What does the FDA's 2026 proposal to remove GLP-1 drugs from the 503B compounding list mean for patients?
fda-compounded-glp1-503b-proposal.answerHtml: On April 30, 2026, the FDA proposed removing semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list, which has allowed large-scale outsourcing-facility compounding for telehealth distribution. With brand-name products (Wegovy, Ozempic, Zepbound, Mounjaro) no longer in shortage, the FDA found no qualifying clinical need. The proposal does not immediately stop all compounding — narrow patient-specific 503A compounding remains permitted. FDA safety data (2026) document over 100 hospitalizations and at least 10 deaths linked to compounded semaglutide, primarily from dosing errors. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

genital-herpes-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat genital herpes (HSV-2)?
genital-herpes-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Genital herpes (HSV-2) affects approximately 12% of U.S. adults aged 14–49. The 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines recommend valacyclovir 1 g PO BID for 7–10 days for first-episode treatment (acyclovir 400 mg TID for 7–10 days is an alternative). Suppressive therapy — valacyclovir 1 g daily — reduces recurrence by 70–80% and lowers transmission risk by ~48% in discordant couples. Episodic therapy (valacyclovir 500 mg BID × 3 days) shortens recurrent outbreaks. Asymptomatic shedding drives most transmission; condoms combined with antivirals reduce but do not eliminate risk. In pregnancy, start suppressive therapy at 36 weeks; ACOG guidelines (2026) recommend cesarean if active lesions are present. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

genital-warts-guide.question: What is the best treatment for genital warts (HPV) in 2026?
genital-warts-guide.answerHtml: Anogenital warts, caused primarily by human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11, are one of the most common sexually transmitted infections. The CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines recommend a menu of effective options, and treatment choice is driven by wart location, size, patient preference, and cost. Patient-applied options include imiquimod 5% cream (complete clearance in ~51% of patients, NNT 2.2 vs placebo), podofilox 0.5% solution (~45% clearance), and sinecatechins 15% ointment (Veregen) (~57% clearance, with the lowest recurrence rate of any topical). Provider-applied options include cryotherapy (~75% clearance) and trichloroacetic acid (TCA) 80 to 90% (~70% clearance). All treatments have a recurrence rate of 30 to 70%. The Gardasil 9 HPV vaccine prevents ~90% of anogenital warts and is FDA-approved through age 45. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth, can prescribe topical therapies and coordinate provider-applied treatment when needed.

gig-worker-healthcare-options.question: What are the healthcare options for gig workers without employer insurance?
gig-worker-healthcare-options.answerHtml: An estimated 57 million Americans participate in the gig economy without employer-sponsored health benefits, and independent workers are nearly twice as likely to be uninsured as traditionally employed people (Commonwealth Fund, 2023). Realistic options include ACA Marketplace plans — subsidized based on income, available at HealthCare.gov — and Medicaid for those earning at or below 138% of the federal poverty level in expansion states. Health sharing ministries and short-term plans carry material risks as unregulated products. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

glp-1-weight-loss-oral-medication-guide.question: What are the GLP-1 weight loss medications available in 2026, including oral options?
glp-1-weight-loss-oral-medication-guide.answerHtml: GLP-1 receptor agonists produce 15–20% body weight reduction in trials, rivaling bariatric surgery. The FDA approved Foundayo (orforglipron) in April 2026 as the first oral GLP-1 without fasting restrictions; phase 3 trials showed 12.4% weight loss at 72 weeks (NEJM, 2026). Injectable tirzepatide achieves up to 20% weight loss per SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM). A boxed warning applies for thyroid C-cell tumors; contraindicated in medullary thyroid cancer history. Without continued therapy, 60–80% of lost weight returns. Self-pay starts at approximately $149/month for Foundayo. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

gout-guide.question: What is the best treatment for gout in 2026?
gout-guide.answerHtml: Acute gout flares are treated promptly with an anti-inflammatory selected for the person’s medical history: low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg one hour later), an NSAID at an anti-inflammatory dose, or a short oral corticosteroid course. Long-term control requires urate-lowering therapy when indicated, usually allopurinol started low and titrated to serum urate below 6 mg/dL, or below 5 mg/dL with tophi. The 2020 ACR guideline strongly recommends urate-lowering therapy for tophi, gout-related radiographic damage, or two or more flares yearly. Before allopurinol, people of Southeast Asian or African American ancestry should discuss HLA-B*58:01 testing because the allele is associated with severe skin reactions. A first hot, swollen joint or fever needs urgent in-person assessment to exclude infection.

hair-loss-male-pattern-guide.question: What is the best treatment for male pattern hair loss in 2026?
hair-loss-male-pattern-guide.answerHtml: For most men with androgenetic alopecia (male pattern hair loss), the highest-yield regimen in 2026 is combination therapy with oral finasteride 1 mg daily plus topical minoxidil 5% twice daily. In the AAD 2024 guidelines, both are strongly recommended as first-line pharmacologic options, and combination therapy outperforms either monotherapy for hair density and long-term stabilization. Emerging evidence supports low-dose oral minoxidil (2.5 to 5 mg daily) as an alternative for men who cannot tolerate topical minoxidil (Skin Appendage Disord 2023 review; Panchaprateep 2020). Results take 6 to 12 months to become visible, and discontinuation reverses gains within 6 to 12 months. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth, can start finasteride and minoxidil after reviewing medical history.

head-lice-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat head lice, especially when OTC treatments fail?
head-lice-treatment-guide.answerHtml: An estimated 6–12 million head lice infestations occur in the US annually, primarily in children ages 3–11 (CDC). First-line OTC treatment is permethrin 1% (Nix), but up to 77% of lice worldwide carry pyrethroid resistance mutations, causing frequent OTC failures (AAP Head Lice Guidance, 2022). When OTC treatment fails, prescriptions—spinosad 0.9%, benzyl alcohol 5%, topical ivermectin 0.5%, or malathion 0.5%—remain effective against resistant lice. The AAP opposes no-nit school exclusion policies. Household decontamination should be targeted; no pesticide sprays are needed. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

hyperhidrosis-guide.question: What is the best treatment for hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating) in 2026?
hyperhidrosis-guide.answerHtml: Hyperhidrosis affects an estimated 4.8% of Americans (about 15.3 million adults), yet only 1 in 6 receives active treatment (Doolittle et al., Arch Dermatol Res 2016). The International Hyperhidrosis Society stepwise algorithm anchors first-line therapy on aluminum chloride 20% topical for mild-to-moderate axillary, palmar, or plantar disease. For patients who fail topical antiperspirant or have severe disease (HDSS score 3 or 4), botulinum toxin A (axillae, palms, soles) and iontophoresis (palms, soles) are strong second-line options, while topical glycopyrronium (Qbrexza) is FDA-approved for axillary hyperhidrosis in patients aged 9 and older. Oral oxybutynin is a low-cost option for generalized or refractory disease. miraDry (microwave thermolysis) and endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy are permanent-effect options reserved for treatment-resistant cases. Every serious attempt at treating excessive sweating starts with confirming primary versus secondary hyperhidrosis. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth, can start most first-line and second-line therapies without an in-person visit.

hypertension-blood-pressure-guide.question: How is hypertension treated, and when can I get a blood pressure medication refill via telehealth?
hypertension-blood-pressure-guide.answerHtml: Nearly 48% of US adults have hypertension but only 1 in 4 have it under control—medication adherence is the most critical factor (AHA/ACC 2025 Guidelines). Targets are BP below 130/80 mmHg for most adults, with first-line agents including thiazides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and calcium channel blockers. Lifestyle changes—DASH diet, sodium below 2,300 mg/day, exercise—lower systolic BP by 5–20 mmHg (NHLBI DASH). A BP above 180/120 with symptoms is a hypertensive emergency requiring the ER. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

hypothyroidism-treatment-guide.question: How is hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, and how should TSH be monitored?
hypothyroidism-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Hypothyroidism affects roughly 5% of the US population; Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause (ATA 2014 Guidelines). Levothyroxine is first-line treatment—standard dosing is 1.6 mcg/kg/day, starting lower in older adults and those with cardiac disease. Recheck TSH 6–8 weeks after any dose change; annual monitoring with target TSH 0.5–2.5 mIU/L suffices once stable (AAFP Thyroid Management). Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before food, separated by 4 hours from calcium, iron, and PPIs. Pregnant women need an immediate 25–30% dose increase at confirmed conception. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

international-visitor-medical-care-guide.question: What should international visitors do if they get sick in the United States?
international-visitor-medical-care-guide.answerHtml: About 62.4 million international visitors travel to the United States each year (U.S. National Travel and Tourism Office), and a meaningful share get sick during the trip. The US has no universal healthcare system, so visitors navigate four main access points: 911 for life-threatening emergencies, the emergency department for genuine emergencies, urgent care for same-day non-emergencies, and telehealth for conditions that do not require an in-person exam. Choosing correctly matters because an uninsured ER visit runs roughly $1,200 to $3,000, while urgent care typically costs $150 to $280 and telehealth $50 to $150 (KFF 2022). Under federal law, most US healthcare facilities must provide qualified interpreters at no cost (HHS Section 1557). Foreign prescriptions are not valid in the US; a US-licensed clinician must write a new one, and foreign visitors may bring up to 50 dosage units of controlled substances for personal use in their original labeled containers (DEA guidance). Travelers’ diarrhea (attack rates 30 to 70 percent over two weeks abroad; Barrett and Brown, BMJ 2016), respiratory infections, UTIs, minor injuries, and prescription refills are the most common reasons visitors seek care and can often be handled outside the ER.

latisse-guide.question: How does Latisse (bimatoprost) work for eyelash growth, and does it actually work?
latisse-guide.answerHtml: Latisse (bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03%) is the only FDA-approved prescription treatment for eyelash hypotrichosis (inadequate or not enough lashes), approved by the FDA in December 2008. It is a synthetic prostaglandin analog originally developed for glaucoma. Applied once nightly to the upper eyelid margin with a sterile applicator, bimatoprost extends the anagen (growth) phase of the eyelash hair cycle and increases hair follicle number and pigmentation. In the pivotal Phase 3 trial of 278 adults with minimal or moderate eyelash prominence, 78% of bimatoprost-treated patients achieved at least a one-grade improvement on the Global Eyelash Assessment at 16 weeks, versus 18% with vehicle (Smith et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2012). Eyelash length increased 25%, thickness 106%, and darkness 18% over vehicle. Effects are dose-dependent on continued use; discontinuation returns eyelashes to baseline in 8 to 12 weeks. Common side effects are eyelid pruritus, conjunctival hyperemia, dry eye, and eyelid hyperpigmentation, all generally mild and reversible. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth, can prescribe Latisse after reviewing eye health and medical history.

malaria-prophylaxis-guide.question: What is the difference between Malarone and doxycycline for malaria prevention?
malaria-prophylaxis-guide.answerHtml: Both atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) and doxycycline are first-line options for chloroquine-resistant malaria per the CDC malaria drug-selection guidelines. The primary difference is post-trip duration: Malarone continues for only 7 days after leaving the malaria zone (ideal for shorter trips), while doxycycline requires 4 full weeks after return — the most common adherence failure. Doxycycline is substantially less expensive and is preferred for Thai border regions. Key contraindications differ: doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy (all trimesters) and children under 8; Malarone is avoided in severe renal impairment. Doxycycline requires daily SPF 30+ sunscreen due to photosensitivity. Per the DailyMed doxycycline label, both begin 1–2 days before entering the malaria zone.

managing-blood-pressure-mobile-workers.question: How can truck drivers and mobile workers manage high blood pressure while on the road?
managing-blood-pressure-mobile-workers.answerHtml: Hypertension affects 26–35% of commercial truck drivers—roughly double the general working population—and is the leading cause of FMCSA medical disqualification (FMCSA Medical Standards). DOT thresholds: BP below 140/90 earns a 2-year certificate; 160/100–179/109 earns 1 year; at or above 180/110 results in disqualification. Once-daily medications—amlodipine, lisinopril, losartan, chlorthalidone—fit variable schedules better than twice-daily regimens (AHA/ACC 2025 Guidelines). Sodium reduction is the highest-yield dietary change; average truck-stop meals contain 2,000–3,500 mg per sitting. BP above 180/120 with symptoms is an ER emergency. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

mastitis-treatment-guide.question: How is mastitis treated, and should you continue breastfeeding?
mastitis-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Mastitis exists on a spectrum from inflammatory to bacterial; the ABM Protocol #36 (2022) moved away from reflexive antibiotics for early inflammatory cases. Continue breastfeeding—it is safe for your infant and is a cornerstone of treatment; stopping worsens the condition. When antibiotics are needed (fever >38.5°C or worsening after 12–24 hours), first-line treatment is dicloxacillin 500 mg QID or cephalexin 500 mg QID for 10–14 days, covering Staphylococcus aureus (ACOG). Breast abscess develops in 3–11% of cases and requires ultrasound plus drainage, not antibiotics alone. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

medical-care-visitors-from-india-guide.question: How can a visitor from India keep their prescriptions and chronic conditions on track during a US trip?
medical-care-visitors-from-india-guide.answerHtml: For the 2.2 million visitors who traveled from India to the US in 2024 (NTTO 2024), the two most common medical questions are how to keep a chronic-condition regimen intact and whether a foreign prescription can be filled here. The short answers are: your WHO INN generic names (levothyroxine, amlodipine, atorvastatin, metformin) are what a US pharmacist recognizes, not your Indian brand names; a US-licensed clinician must write any new US prescription; under the FDA Personal Importation Policy foreign nationals may bring a 90-day supply of their medications for personal use; and a same-day US telehealth visit can typically bridge non-controlled chronic medications (blood pressure, thyroid, oral diabetes, statins) for a stable visitor. Several drugs commonly prescribed in India are Schedule IV controlled substances in the US (Restyl / alprazolam, Modalert / modafinil, clonazepam, diazepam) and are governed by the DEA 50-dosage-unit personal-import rule (DEA 2026); some (Nitrosun / nitrazepam, Rohypnol / flunitrazepam) are not FDA-approved and cannot be prescribed in the US at all. For older visiting parents the clinical picture also matters: South Asians in the US have 23% age-adjusted diabetes prevalence compared with 6% in non-Hispanic Whites (Kanaya et al. 2014 MASALA/MESA study), diabetes is diagnosed about 10 years earlier (CDC 2015), and Asian Indian ancestry is now a formal "risk-enhancing factor" in the 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guidelines.

medical-care-visitors-from-mexico-guide.question: How can a visitor from Mexico keep their prescriptions and chronic conditions on track during a US trip?
medical-care-visitors-from-mexico-guide.answerHtml: For the 13.4 million Mexican land visitors and growing air arrivals who came to the US in 2024 (NTTO 2024), a Mexican prescription cannot be filled at a US pharmacy but a same-day US telehealth visit can typically bridge non-controlled chronic medications (blood pressure, thyroid, oral diabetes, statins, most inhalers) for a stable visitor. Under the FDA Personal Importation Policy foreign nationals may bring or ship a 90-day supply of drug products for personal use, and this rule is enforced at Southwest border ports. Some medications commonly prescribed in Mexico are US Schedule IV controlled substances (Rivotril / clonazepam, Tafil / alprazolam, Ambien / zolpidem, Tramadol) that follow the DEA 50-dosage-unit personal-import rule (DEA). A few common Mexican medications are not FDA-approved and cannot be prescribed in the US (Lercadip / lercanidipine, and Mexican combination products like Fluoxac / fluoxetine plus olanzapine combinations). For older Mexican-American and visiting Mexican adults, diagnosed diabetes prevalence is 11.1% (2019-2021), the highest among Hispanic subgroups per CDC 2024 National Diabetes Statistics Report, and the age-standardized prevalence including undiagnosed diabetes is 20.1% among Mexican-American adults (O'Brien et al. 2014 Prev Chronic Dis). US hospitals receiving federal funding must provide qualified Spanish interpreter services free of charge under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act (HHS OCR 2024 final rule, effective July 5, 2025).

migraine-treatment-guide.question: What are the best treatments for migraines, including prevention?
migraine-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Migraine is the leading cause of disability in adults under 50 (Lancet Neurology, GBD 2016). For acute attacks, sumatriptan (triptan class) is first-line for moderate-to-severe migraine—treat at the first sign of pain per AHS 2024 consensus guidelines. Using triptans 10+ days/month or NSAIDs 15+ days/month for over 3 months causes medication overuse headache. Preventive therapy is indicated at 4+ headache days per month; CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) are first-line preventive options per AHS 2024. A sudden thunderclap headache requires ER evaluation. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

motion-sickness-treatment-guide.question: What is the best treatment and prevention for motion sickness?
motion-sickness-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Motion sickness results from sensory conflict between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive systems; roughly one-third of people are highly susceptible (CDC Yellow Book, 2024). The scopolamine transdermal patch 1.5 mg is the most effective agent for extended travel—apply behind the ear at least 4 hours before departure for 72-hour protection (FDA Transderm Scop). For shorter trips, meclizine 25–50 mg or dimenhydrinate 50 mg taken 30–60 minutes before travel are practical OTC choices. Non-drug strategies—horizon fixation, P6 acupressure, ginger—are effective with no side effects. If dizziness occurs with head position changes rather than during travel, consider BPPV, which requires separate evaluation. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

paxlovid-2026-efficacy-update.question: Does Paxlovid still work in 2026, and who benefits most?
paxlovid-2026-efficacy-update.answerHtml: Real-world data from 703,647 patients show Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) reduced hospitalization by 39% and death by 61%, including in vaccinated patients against current Omicron subvariants (Xie et al., PLoS Medicine, 2025). Absolute benefit depends on baseline risk—for a healthy vaccinated adult under 50, absolute risk reduction may be as small as 1.3% (Science analysis). Viral rebound occurs in ~21% of recipients but is mild and self-limited; retreatment offers no clinical benefit. Nirmatrelvir resistance remains rare. Treatment must begin within 5 days of symptom onset. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

performance-anxiety-treatment-guide.question: How is performance anxiety treated, and can I get propranolol via telehealth?
performance-anxiety-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Performance anxiety—racing heart, tremor, voice wavering before a high-stakes event—responds well to propranolol 10–40 mg taken 30–60 minutes before the triggering event (StatPearls: Beta-Blockers in Anxiety). Propranolol blocks peripheral sympathetic symptoms without sedation or dependence risk, making it preferable to benzodiazepines (AAFP, 2023). Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma, significant bradycardia, and decompensated heart failure. Situational performance anxiety and social anxiety disorder (SAD) are distinct—propranolol alone is insufficient for SAD, which requires CBT and/or SSRIs. A physician review is required. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

pink-eye-adults-antibiotics-vs-watchful-.question: Do adults with pink eye need antibiotic eye drops, or is watchful waiting appropriate?
pink-eye-adults-antibiotics-vs-watchful-.answerHtml: Up to 80% of adult pink eye cases are viral, and antibiotic eye drops provide no benefit for viral conjunctivitis, per a Cochrane review of 21 RCTs (8,805 eyes) (2024). Even bacterial conjunctivitis is self-limited in roughly 60% of cases without treatment. AAFP guidelines support watchful waiting for uncomplicated bacterial cases. Reserve antibiotic drops (e.g., erythromycin ointment or polymyxin-trimethoprim) for confirmed bacterial infection with persistent mucopurulent discharge. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

pink-eye-conjunctivitis-guide.question: What is pink eye (conjunctivitis) and how is it treated?
pink-eye-conjunctivitis-guide.answerHtml: Pink eye (conjunctivitis) affects approximately 6 million Americans annually and is classified as viral (up to 80% of cases), bacterial, or allergic. The 2024 American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern recommends against routine antibiotic prescribing, as most cases resolve without treatment. Viral conjunctivitis is managed with cool compresses and artificial tears; bacterial cases with persistent mucopurulent discharge may warrant antibiotic drops; allergic conjunctivitis responds to antihistamine drops. Red flags requiring urgent in-person care include vision change, severe pain, or corneal involvement. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

poison-ivy-oak-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a poison ivy, oak, or sumac rash?
poison-ivy-oak-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Urushiol — the oily resin in poison ivy, oak, and sumac — triggers a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction in roughly 85% of exposed individuals. Washing skin with soap and water within 10–15 minutes meaningfully reduces rash severity. Mild rashes respond to over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream and oral antihistamines; moderate-to-severe or widespread rashes (face, genitals, >10% BSA) require oral prednisone — typically 40–60 mg/day tapered over 14–21 days — per AAD guidance. Inhaled smoke from burning plants is a medical emergency. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

psoriasis-treatment-guide.question: How is psoriasis treated according to current clinical guidelines?
psoriasis-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Psoriasis treatment follows the AAD-NPF joint guidelines (2019–2021), which recommend a stepwise approach: topical corticosteroids (e.g., clobetasol propionate 0.05% for thick plaques) and vitamin D analogues (calcipotriene) for mild disease; phototherapy for moderate disease; and biologics targeting IL-17, IL-23, or TNF-α pathways for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, achieving complete clearance in the majority of qualifying patients. PASI scoring guides therapy escalation (2020). Psoriatic arthritis screening is essential, as it develops in up to 30% of patients. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

rosacea-treatment-guide.question: How is rosacea treated based on current guidelines?
rosacea-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Rosacea is an inflammatory vascular disease managed with phenotype-based therapy per AAD and National Rosacea Society guidelines. For inflammatory papules and pustules, topical ivermectin 1% cream (Soolantra) has outperformed metronidazole in head-to-head trials; published data (2024) confirm superior lesion reduction. Persistent erythema responds to brimonidine gel. Moderate-to-severe cases benefit from low-dose doxycycline 40 mg modified-release (Oracea) as an anti-inflammatory — not antibiotic — agent. Severe rhinophyma or laser-requiring cases need in-person dermatology. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

running-out-of-medication-visiting-us-gu.question: What should an international visitor do if they run out of medication in the United States?
running-out-of-medication-visiting-us-gu.answerHtml: International visitors who run out of a chronic medication during a US trip cannot fill a foreign prescription at a US pharmacy. A US-licensed clinician must write a new US prescription, and a same-day physician-led telehealth visit is usually the fastest path for non-controlled medications like blood pressure pills, thyroid hormone, oral diabetes drugs, most asthma inhalers, statins, birth control pills, and most SSRIs. Under the FDA Personal Importation Policy, foreign nationals may bring or ship a 90-day supply of their medication for personal use, and visitors staying longer can have additional supply mailed. Foreign visitors may also bring up to 50 dosage units of controlled substances (opioids, benzodiazepines, ADHD stimulants, sleep medications) in the original labeled container per DEA guidance (DEA 2026). DEA telemedicine flexibilities extended through December 31, 2026 now allow DEA-registered US clinicians to prescribe Schedule II-V controlled medications via audio-video telemedicine without a prior in-person visit, but individual telehealth companies often apply stricter internal rules and frequently decline controlled prescriptions for visitors. Generic prices at US pharmacies are typically low (common blood pressure, thyroid, and diabetes generics often run $4 to $20 for a 30-day supply on GoodRx).

scabies-treatment-guide.question: How is scabies diagnosed and treated?
scabies-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Scabies is a highly contagious skin infestation caused by Sarcoptes scabiei. First-line treatment per CDC guidelines is permethrin 5% cream applied neck-to-toe, left on 8–14 hours, and repeated one week later; oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg (off-label) with a repeat dose at 7–14 days is an effective alternative. All household members and close contacts must be treated simultaneously. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies requires combination oral ivermectin plus permethrin — often 3–7 courses — and warrants in-person evaluation. Post-treatment itch lasting 2–4 weeks is normal and does not indicate failure. AAD guidance (2026) supports virtual visits for classic presentations. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

seasonal-allergies-guide.question: How are seasonal allergies (allergic rhinitis) treated?
seasonal-allergies-guide.answerHtml: Seasonal allergic rhinitis affects approximately 82 million Americans (2024 CDC data) — about 1 in 4 adults. First-line therapy per AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameters includes intranasal corticosteroid sprays (fluticasone or mometasone) and second-generation oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, or fexofenadine) with minimal sedation. The 2024–2025 ARIA-EAACI guideline revision now favors combination intranasal antihistamine + corticosteroid (e.g., azelastine-fluticasone) as first-line for moderate-to-severe symptoms. Allergen immunotherapy is appropriate for patients with inadequate pharmacotherapy response. A licensed clinician — reached via telehealth or an in-person visit — provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

seasonal-allergy-guidelines-2026.question: What changed in the 2026 seasonal allergy treatment guidelines?
seasonal-allergy-guidelines-2026.answerHtml: In April 2026, the ARIA-EAACI initiative published its most significant allergy guideline update since 2010, now recommending combination intranasal antihistamine + corticosteroid sprays (INAH+INCS) — such as azelastine-fluticasone — as first-line therapy over either monotherapy for moderate-to-severe seasonal allergic rhinitis, per the 2026 ARIA guidelines. A 2024 network meta-analysis of 151 studies in JACI identified fluticasone furoate and fluticasone propionate as highest-performing intranasal corticosteroids. First-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine) are now discouraged. Climate data show pollen seasons now average 21 days longer than in 1970. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

shingles-antiviral-window-guide.question: What is the 72-hour window for shingles treatment?
shingles-antiviral-window-guide.answerHtml: The first 72 hours after a shingles rash starts is the time period most directly studied for oral antiviral treatment. Valacyclovir 1 gram three times daily for 7 days is a common regimen; acyclovir and famciclovir are alternatives. Do not wait for the clock if new blisters are forming or the rash affects the eye, face, ear, immune system, or nervous system. The valacyclovir trial and ophthalmic shingles guidance explain why timing and location both matter.

shingles-guide.question: How is shingles treated, and what is the 72-hour antiviral window?
shingles-guide.answerHtml: Shingles is a painful, one-sided rash caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus. Oral antiviral treatment is best studied when started within 72 hours after rash onset. Valacyclovir, acyclovir, and famciclovir are options; eye, face, ear, widespread, neurologic, and immunocompromised cases need in-person evaluation. The valacyclovir trial and ACIP recommendations support prompt treatment and prevention with Shingrix when eligible.

shingles-vaccine-guide.question: Who should get Shingrix, and how effective is the shingles vaccine?
shingles-vaccine-guide.answerHtml: Shingrix is the preferred U.S. shingles vaccine for immunocompetent adults age 50 and older and immunocompromised adults age 19 and older. It is a two-dose, non-live vaccine. Pivotal trials found 97.2% efficacy against shingles in adults age 50 and older and 91.3% in pooled adults age 70 and older. ACIP guidance and the ZOE-50 trial provide the core evidence.

sinus-infection-guide.question: What is the best way to treat a sinus infection in 2026?
sinus-infection-guide.answerHtml: Watchful waiting is now the recommended first move for uncomplicated acute bacterial rhinosinusitis when follow-up is available, per the 2025 AAO-HNS Adult Sinusitis Update. Most acute sinus infections are viral, and the 2018 Cochrane review concluded antibiotics offer only marginal benefit in uncomplicated cases. A bacterial pattern is more likely when purulent nasal drainage plus nasal blockage or facial pressure persists 10 days without improvement, or symptoms worsen after initial improvement. Symptom care can include saline irrigation and an intranasal corticosteroid. If an antibiotic is needed, the 2025 update lists amoxicillin with or without clavulanate for 5 to 7 days as first line. A licensed clinician, whether through telehealth or in-person care, can assess the pattern, allergy history, and urgent warning signs.

smoking-cessation-guide.question: What is the best treatment for smoking cessation in 2026?
smoking-cessation-guide.answerHtml: For most adults who smoke, the highest-yield combination in 2026 is varenicline plus behavioral support for 12 weeks, with combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus lozenge or gum) as the strongest over-the-counter alternative. In the head-to-head EAGLES trial (n=8,144), 6-month continuous abstinence was 21.8% with varenicline vs 15.7% with the nicotine patch, 16.2% with bupropion, and 9.4% with placebo. A 2023 Cochrane review confirms combination NRT is superior to any single form (high-certainty evidence, RR 1.27). The FDA removed varenicline’s boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events in December 2016, and it is now considered safe in patients with stable psychiatric illness. Adding structured behavioral support, even a free quitline call, roughly doubles the effect of medication alone per the USPSTF 2021 evidence review (pooled RR 1.83). Cytisinicline, an investigational partial agonist with a favorable safety profile, has an FDA PDUFA date of June 20, 2026. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review symptoms, screen for contraindications, and prescribe appropriate therapy.

sore-throat-guide.question: Does a sore throat need antibiotics, and how do you know if it's strep?
sore-throat-guide.answerHtml: Up to 85–90% of adult sore throats are viral; antibiotics provide no benefit for viral pharyngitis. Group A Streptococcus accounts for 5–15% of adult cases, per 2025 IDSA strep throat guidelines. Clinical scoring using the Centor/McIsaac criteria guides rapid strep testing; positive results warrant antibiotic treatment. Published data (2013) confirm penicillin and amoxicillin remain first-line — Group A Strep has shown zero penicillin resistance in over 90 years. Standard adult dosing is amoxicillin 500 mg twice daily or 1,000 mg once daily × 10 days. Red flags (trismus, uvular deviation, drooling) suggest peritonsillar abscess requiring ER care. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

telehealth-acne-eczema-dermatology-evide.question: Is telehealth effective for treating acne and eczema?
telehealth-acne-eczema-dermatology-evide.answerHtml: Published clinical evidence confirms teledermatology produces outcomes comparable to in-person care for both acne and eczema. A 2024 systematic review of 21 studies in the Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery found an 87.94% reduction in acne GAGS severity scores via telehealth, with 75.2% concordance with face-to-face assessments and 71.8% of patients preferring video visits for future care. For eczema, a JAMA Dermatology RCT (2021) found teledermatology non-inferior to in-person evaluation for atopic dermatitis management. Conditions requiring biopsy or patch testing need in-person referral. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

telehealth-cold-sores-antiviral-timing.question: When should you take antivirals for a cold sore, and how does telehealth help?
telehealth-cold-sores-antiviral-timing.answerHtml: The single most important factor in cold sore treatment is timing: antivirals must be started within 24–48 hours of the first prodrome symptom (tingling, burning) before visible lesions form. The CDC STI Treatment Guidelines state episodic therapy is most effective when initiated within 1 day of symptom onset. High-dose 1-day valacyclovir — 2 g at first symptom, repeated 12 hours later — reduced episode duration by approximately 1 day in two large RCTs (~2,000 patients); famciclovir 1,500 mg single dose is an effective alternative. In-person appointment wait times often exceed this window. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

telehealth-ear-infections-adults.question: Can you treat an ear infection over telehealth?
telehealth-ear-infections-adults.answerHtml: Most adult ear infections — both otitis externa (swimmer's ear) and otitis media — can be safely diagnosed and treated via telehealth. A 2025 trial of 200 acute otitis media patients found telehealth follow-up achieved ear pain relief in 84% of cases, equivalent to in-person care (P=0.57), per published outcomes data. A 2026 scoping review found smartphone-based telehealth handled 83% of ENT referrals remotely. The AAO-HNS guideline (2024) recommends topical eardrops — not oral amoxicillin — for uncomplicated otitis externa. Red flags requiring in-person care include facial swelling, hearing loss, or immunocompromise. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

telehealth-sinusitis-virtual-care.question: Can a sinus infection be treated via telehealth?
telehealth-sinusitis-virtual-care.answerHtml: Yes — and telehealth often produces better antibiotic stewardship than in-person care. A 2019 study in Open Forum Infectious Diseases found virtual visits produced guideline-concordant sinusitis diagnoses 69.1% of the time versus 45.7% in-office (P<0.001), with fewer unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions (68.6% vs. 94.3%). The 2025 AAO-HNSF guidelines recommend watchful waiting as initial management for suspected bacterial sinusitis; when antibiotics are indicated, amoxicillin with or without clavulanate for 5–7 days is first-line. Symptoms persisting >10 days, severe unilateral pain, periorbital swelling, or altered mental status warrant in-person evaluation. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

telehealth-uti-clinical-evidence.question: What does the clinical evidence show about telehealth for UTI treatment?
telehealth-uti-clinical-evidence.answerHtml: Published evidence strongly supports telehealth UTI care. A 2023 analysis of 51,474 women in a national telehealth UTI program (PLOS ONE) found 89.5% symptom resolution — comparable to in-person benchmarks — with 94% adherence to IDSA antibiotic protocols. A 2026 PLOS Digital Health systematic review confirmed no significant prescribing difference between virtual and in-person UTI visits across 18 studies. Telehealth is appropriate for uncomplicated UTIs in non-pregnant women aged 18–65 without comorbidities; first-line agents include nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID ×5 days or TMP-SMX DS BID ×3 days. Red flags — fever >101°F, flank pain, or pregnancy — require in-person care. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

tick-bite-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a tick bite and prevent Lyme disease?
tick-bite-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Remove the tick with fine-tipped tweezers promptly; Borrelia burgdorferi transmission typically requires ≥36 hours of attachment. Per the 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR Lyme disease guidelines, a single oral dose of doxycycline 200 mg reduces Lyme risk by ~87% when all four criteria are met: Ixodes tick, endemic area, attachment ≥36 hours, prophylaxis within 72 hours. The CDC recorded 62,551 confirmed Lyme cases in 2022. An expanding erythema migrans rash warrants doxycycline 100 mg BID ×10–14 days without waiting for serology. Rocky Mountain spotted fever requires immediate doxycycline — delays can be fatal. Seek the ER for petechial rash, high fever, or meningismus. Telehealth is appropriate for prophylaxis assessment and early Lyme management. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

tinea-ringworm-guide.question: How do you treat ringworm and other tinea fungal skin infections?
tinea-ringworm-guide.answerHtml: Tinea (ringworm) is caused by dermatophytes and treatment depends on location. For tinea corporis and cruris, topical terbinafine 1% once daily ×1–2 weeks is first-line per AAD guidelines; clotrimazole 1% BID ×2–4 weeks is an alternative. Tinea capitis requires systemic therapy — topical antifungals cannot penetrate the hair follicle. In the US (T. tonsurans >89% of cases), oral terbinafine is preferred; griseofulvin 20–25 mg/kg/day ×6–12 weeks for Microsporum species. Onychomycosis: oral terbinafine 250 mg daily ×12 weeks (toenails). Avoid combination steroid-antifungal creams — steroids suppress inflammation while the fungus spreads (tinea incognito). Telehealth is appropriate for body and groin tinea; scalp infections and nail fungus can also be initiated virtually. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

tinea-versicolor-guide.question: How do you treat tinea versicolor and why does skin discoloration persist after treatment?
tinea-versicolor-guide.answerHtml: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia yeast — not a dermatophyte — so oral terbinafine is ineffective. First-line treatment per AAD clinical guidance is ketoconazole 2% or selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo applied to dry skin ×5–10 minutes daily ×1–2 weeks. For extensive disease, oral fluconazole 300 mg weekly ×2 doses or itraconazole 200 mg daily ×7 days are alternatives. Skin discoloration persists weeks to months after mycologic cure because azelaic acid from Malassezia metabolism inhibits melanocyte tyrosinase — color normalizes as melanocytes recover. Recurrence affects 60% within 12 months; monthly prophylaxis with ketoconazole 2% shampoo reduces relapse. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

travel-medicine-guide.question: What prescriptions do I need before international travel?
travel-medicine-guide.answerHtml: A pre-travel medicine visit addresses four core pharmacological prevention needs per the CDC Yellow Book pre-travel consultation guidelines: (1) malaria prophylaxis — atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) or doxycycline for chloroquine-resistant destinations; (2) traveler's diarrhea standby — azithromycin (preferred over ciprofloxacin for South/Southeast Asia due to fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter); (3) altitude sickness prevention — acetazolamide 125 mg BID for moderate-altitude destinations per the CDC Yellow Book altitude guidelines; and (4) motion sickness prevention. Yellow fever vaccines, primaquine, and tafenoquine require an in-person travel clinic. All prescriptions are non-controlled; self-pay option starts at $79.

tretinoin-guide.question: What is the best treatment for photoaging and wrinkles in 2026?
tretinoin-guide.answerHtml: For adults seeking evidence-based prevention and reversal of photoaging (sun-induced wrinkles, hyperpigmentation, and skin roughness), the two highest-yield interventions in 2026 are daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen and prescription tretinoin. Tretinoin is the only topical retinoid FDA-approved for photoaging (approved 1995 for palliative treatment of photodamage; originally approved 1971 for acne). A 2022 systematic review of 7 randomized controlled trials confirmed tretinoin significantly improves wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines, with measurable effects at 4 months that continue for at least 24 months. Concentrations of 0.025% and 0.1% produce equivalent efficacy at 48 weeks with significantly less irritation at 0.025%. For patients who cannot tolerate tretinoin, adapalene 0.3% gel is non-inferior (Bagatin 2018). Tretinoin is contraindicated in pregnancy. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can prescribe tretinoin after reviewing skin type, medical history, and photoprotection habits.

truck-driver-health-risks-telehealth.question: What are the biggest health risks for truck drivers and how can telehealth help?
truck-driver-health-risks-telehealth.answerHtml: Truck drivers face disproportionately high chronic disease rates: CDC NIOSH data show hypertension in 26–40%, diabetes at 14.4% (double national prevalence), and obesity (BMI ≥30) in 69% of long-haul drivers. A 2024 BMC Public Health meta-analysis found 61.75% experience musculoskeletal disorders; 44% report depressive symptoms with 80% untreated. Sleep apnea prevalence is 28–50% versus 6–17% in the general population. Telehealth removes the structural barriers — no clinic, no time off route, prescriptions sent to any pharmacy on your route. DOT physicals require an in-person certified Medical Examiner and cannot be completed via telehealth. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

type-2-diabetes-medication-guide.question: What medications are used to manage type 2 diabetes?
type-2-diabetes-medication-guide.answerHtml: The 2025 ADA Standards of Care have substantially shifted type 2 diabetes treatment. For patients with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, tirzepatide) and SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are now recommended independent of A1C. Tirzepatide produced a mean A1C reduction of 1.3% and 10.2 kg weight loss at 12 months versus 0.9% and 6.1 kg for semaglutide in real-world data. Metformin remains first-line for patients without those comorbidities. A1C target is <7% for most adults; individualize for elderly patients. DKA (fruity breath, vomiting) and severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL with altered consciousness) require emergency care. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

urinary-tract-infection-uti-guide.question: What are UTI symptoms, causes, and treatments?
urinary-tract-infection-uti-guide.answerHtml: UTIs account for over 8 million annual U.S. office visits, with E. coli causing 80–85% of cases. The classic triad — dysuria, frequency, urgency — carries >90% positive predictive value in premenopausal women per IDSA guidelines. First-line treatment (2025 IDSA update): nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID ×5 days or TMP-SMX DS BID ×3 days; fosfomycin 3 g single dose is an alternative. Fluoroquinolones are no longer recommended for uncomplicated cystitis. For recurrent UTIs, the 2025 AUA/CUA/SUFU guidelines prioritize vaginal estrogen (postmenopausal), cranberry supplements (≥36 mg PACs daily), and methenamine hippurate before antibiotic prophylaxis. Fever, flank pain, or vomiting suggest pyelonephritis — seek urgent care. Uncomplicated lower UTIs are telehealth-appropriate. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

vaginal-dryness-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat vaginal dryness and genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM)?
vaginal-dryness-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) affects 27–84% of postmenopausal women and worsens without treatment, per the 2020 NAMS Position Statement. First-line: vaginal moisturizers (hyaluronic acid or polycarbophil) every 2–3 days and lubricants during intercourse. For moderate-to-severe symptoms, low-dose vaginal estrogen (cream, tablet, or ring) is most effective; minimal systemic absorption means no progestogen is needed for uterine protection. FDA-approved alternatives include ospemifene 60 mg oral daily (SERM) and prasterone/DHEA vaginal insert. ACOG 2021 guidance supports low-dose vaginal estrogen for most breast cancer survivors at low recurrence risk. Vaginal laser therapy is not recommended outside clinical trials per current evidence. A licensed clinician — accessible via telehealth or in-person care — can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

visby-at-home-sti-pcr-test-review.question: Is the Visby at-home PCR test for STIs accurate and how do you use the results?
visby-at-home-sti-pcr-test-review.answerHtml: The Visby Medical Women's Sexual Health Test — granted FDA De Novo authorization in March 2025 — is the first OTC at-home PCR test for chlamydia, gonorrhea, and trichomoniasis, returning results in ~30 minutes. FDA-reviewed performance data show 96.4–100% sensitivity and 99.6–100% specificity; independent validation in Open Forum Infectious Diseases (January 2025) confirmed ≥95%/≥98% accuracy, "equivalent to centralized lab assays." Chlamydia reaches ~1.6 million annual U.S. cases per CDC STI surveillance. A positive result requires clinician follow-up — do not self-treat. The CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines recommend doxycycline for chlamydia, ceftriaxone for gonorrhea. A negative result does not rule out HIV, syphilis, herpes, or HPV. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

wildfire-smoke-health-guide.question: How do I protect my health from wildfire smoke?
wildfire-smoke-health-guide.answerHtml: Wildfire smoke exposure is largely a PM2.5 problem, and peer-reviewed evidence suggests wildfire PM2.5 is roughly 5 to 10 times more toxic than an equivalent mass of general urban pollution per Aguilera et al., Nature Communications 2021. Monitor fire.airnow.gov and take action at AQI 101 (Orange) if you have asthma, COPD, heart disease, diabetes, are pregnant, or are 65 and older; at AQI 151 (Red) for the general public. Stay indoors, run a MERV-13 or HEPA air cleaner in a designated clean room. A DIY Corsi-Rosenthal box (a 20-inch box fan plus four MERV-13 filters) delivers about 401 CFM of clean-air-delivery in EPA testing, comparable to a $700 commercial HEPA. For necessary outdoor exposure, use a properly fitted NIOSH-approved N95, KN95, or KF94 respirator; cloth and surgical masks provide limited protection. Contact a clinician (telehealth appropriate) for persistent cough, worsening asthma or COPD, or new palpitations or unusual fatigue in someone with heart disease. Call 911 or go to the ER for chest pain, severe shortness of breath, an asthma attack not responding to inhalers, blue lips, or stroke-like symptoms.

yeast-infection-guide.question: How do you diagnose and treat a vaginal yeast infection (vulvovaginal candidiasis)?
yeast-infection-guide.answerHtml: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is caused by Candida albicans in 80–90% of cases; self-diagnosis is unreliable — fewer than 35% of self-diagnosing women have VVC confirmed by laboratory testing (Obstetrics & Gynecology). For uncomplicated VVC, the CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines recommend topical azoles (miconazole 2% or clotrimazole 1% ×3–7 days) with 80–90% cure rates, or a single oral fluconazole 150 mg per IDSA guidelines. Avoid oral fluconazole in pregnancy; use topical clotrimazole ×7 days. For recurrent VVC (≥3 episodes/year), the CDC recommends fluconazole induction ×3 doses, then weekly 100–200 mg ×6 months. If OTC treatment fails, seek clinical evaluation — bacterial vaginosis is a frequent mimic. A licensed clinician — through telehealth or in-person evaluation — can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.
